blocks.text: Update: October 19, 2026

WIRED has reported on our findings. WhatsApp told WIRED that the notes were instructions for its support chatbot, the one people reach when they message WhatsApp Support with AI, and that they showed up in the pages because of a bug that has now been fixed. A WhatsApp spokesperson told WIRED it wants its support chatbots "focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp" and "not to offer legal advice."
Update: October 18, 2026

WhatsApp has removed the hidden notes. Both of the notes quoted below were still on the pages when we checked at 21:40 UTC on October 15. When we checked again at 02:08 UTC on October 18, all 102 hidden blocks were gone from all 80 pages. The help pages are still up. Only the hidden text was taken out.

Copies saved by the Internet Archive still show the notes. Its copy of the delete account page from October 9 has them, and its copy from October 18 doesn't. See it for yourself explains how to check.

blocks.text: To be fair to WhatsApp

inlines.text: To be fair to WhatsApp

blocks.text: There's a reasonable case for some of this, and it should be heard.

inlines.text: There's a reasonable case for some of this, and it should be heard.

blocks.text: A company doesn't want its chatbot giving legal opinions in the company's name. That's sensible, and telling people to see a lawyer is the right call. If the note had stopped at "don't give legal advice", there'd be no story.

blocks.text: It didn't stop there. Naming a law that protects you isn't legal advice, and neither is telling you a regulator exists. The privacy policy already does both. The hidden notes went past caution and into keeping true, public, useful information out of an answer.

blocks.text: WhatsApp may also be right that it can't confirm who owns an account without the phone number, which would make deleting one by request risky. That's a fair reason to say no to a request. It isn't a reason to keep the regulator out of the answer for someone whose request goes nowhere.

blocks.text: WhatsApp didn't keep the notes to itself, though. Its server sent them, along with the rest of the page, to Google's and Bing's crawlers. blocks.text: If you're locked out and want your WhatsApp account gone

inlines.text: If you're locked out and want your WhatsApp account gone

blocks.text: Waiting does work, though WhatsApp's own pages don't agree on how long. The delete account page says an unused account is generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 in the US. The page on inactive account deletion gives one figure with no US exception, and we've seen it say 120 days in one country and 365 in another. Plan on the longer one. If that suits you, you're done.

blocks.text: If it doesn't, you have other routes. You can send WhatsApp an erasure request and see what they say. If you're in the EU and you aren't satisfied, you can complain to your country's data protection authority or to the Irish Data Protection Commission, which is the one WhatsApp's own policy names. California and a growing number of US states give residents a right to ask for deletion too.
